name: pinneapple_orchestration

children.name: pinneapple_orchestration.campaign
children.doc:
A simulation campaign: thousands of runs through one queue, with content addressing, retries and accounting.

Every campaign in this library used to be its own loop — ``apps/aero_optimizer/tools/generate_dataset.py`` ran 436
OpenFOAM jobs in a local process pool, the OpenFOAM campaign module ran a plan file, the factory ran its designs —
and each of them rewrote skipping, retrying and bookkeeping (issue #295). This is that execution layer, once:

* **Content-addressed runs.** A run's key is the SHA-256 of its geometry (the bytes of the file, or of the whole
  directory tree), its solver settings and its conditions. A campaign that is repeated, resumed or run on another
  machine skips every key already done — and a *hit is proven*, not assumed: the stored record is re-read and its
  own key and the hash of its outputs are checked before the run is skipped (``RunCache``). A corrupt record is a
  miss, so the work is redone instead of trusted. Within one campaign the same address is executed once: 2000 cases
  of 25 distinct contents run 25 jobs and answer 1975 rows from them (``source`` says which is which).
* **A queue with retries and timeouts.** A failed run is never dropped: it is recorded with an excerpt of its log
  and a classification (:func:`classify_failure`) — ``mesh``, ``diverged``, ``timeout``, ``setup``, ``crashed`` —
  built on :func:`pinneapple_data.simulation_metadata.openfoam.parse_log`. Only the kinds that can pass on a second
  attempt are retried (``retry_on``, default ``timeout``, ``crashed`` and ``unknown``); a mesh that is wrong or a
  solution that diverges is deterministic and is not retried. Each finished run reaches the cache *before* the queue
  can move on (the backend calls ``on_outcome``), so a process killed mid-campaign loses only what was executing.
* **Backends.** :class:`LocalBackend` (the default), :class:`SlurmBackend` and :class:`CloudBatchBackend` (a cloud
  batch service behind the same ``submit``/``poll`` contract, with the AWS Batch CLI as the provided adapter). All
  three take concurrency, cores per run and cleanup from the same configuration.
* **Accounting with lineage.** ``campaign_report.json`` records wall time, CPU-hours (wall time x cores per run),
  the cache and failure counts with their kinds, and the machine the campaign ran on; ``lineage.json`` writes the
  chain (geometry -> run -> dataset) with :class:`pinneapple_data.lineage.Lineage`.

    import pinneapple as pp
    result = pp.campaign.run(cases, solver, backend="local", workers=8, cache_dir="cache")
    result.rows            # one dict per case: outputs, status, failure kind, log excerpt
    result.report.cpu_hours, result.report.failure_rate
    result.save("runs")    # results.json + campaign_report.json + lineage.json

A solver is anything the campaign can call per case: an object with ``run(params, workdir) -> mapping`` (the
laboratory's ``Simulator``, unchanged), a plain callable ``(params, workdir) -> mapping``, or a command line (then
the job writes ``outputs.json`` in its workdir). A callable solver runs in a worker thread of this process, so
NumPy and solver subprocesses overlap but pure-Python work does not; command jobs are real processes. That limit is
the reason the command form exists, and it is stated here rather than discovered in a benchmark.

classes.name: CaseGeometry
classes.doc: What a run is made of geometrically: a path (hashed on first use) or a digest already known.

classes.name: Case
classes.doc:
One run: an identifier, a geometry, the parameters, the solver settings and the conditions.

``params`` is what goes into the solver, ``settings`` is how it is configured (discretisation, tolerances, mesh
level) and ``conditions`` is the operating point (inlet velocity, temperature, angle). All three are part of the
key: a run is the hash of exactly these, so nothing that changes the answer can be left out of it.

classes.name: CacheRecord
classes.doc: One finished run as the cache keeps it: proven by its own key and the hash of its outputs.

classes.name: RunCache
classes.doc:
Content-addressed store of finished runs: one JSON per key, validated before it is believed.

A record answers a run only when its key matches the key being asked for, its status is ``done`` and the hash it
carries still matches its own outputs. Anything else (a truncated file, a hand-edited record, a record from
another solver) is a miss and is counted as one: the campaign redoes the work rather than trusting it.

classes.name: Outcome
classes.doc: What came of one attempt: the outputs, or the failure with its class and an excerpt of the log.

classes.name: CommandRunner
classes.doc:
How a backend runs a command: ``argv`` in, a :class:`CommandResult` out. Swapped in tests, and in production
it is ``subprocess`` for the cluster CLI or ``ssh`` for a remote host.

classes.name: Backend
classes.doc:
The only thing a campaign asks of a backend: run these pending jobs, yield outcomes as they finish.

``on_outcome`` is called once per finished run, from whichever thread finished it, *before* the outcome is
yielded: that is what makes a campaign durable. The queue cannot run ahead of the record, so a process killed
mid-campaign loses at most the runs still executing, never the ones already answered.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (jobs: Sequence[Job], solver: Any = None, on_outcome: Callable[[Outcome], None] | None = None) -> Iterator[Outcome]

classes.name: LocalBackend
classes.sig: (workers: int = 4, *, cores_per_run: int = 1, runner: CommandRunner = subprocess_runner, cleanup: bool = True)
classes.doc:
The default backend: ``workers`` threads in this process, one workdir per attempt, cleaned after success.

A callable solver runs in a worker thread, so allocations and solver subprocesses overlap while pure-Python work
does not (state the limit, do not hide it). A job with a ``command`` is a real subprocess and therefore a real
second process. A callable that outlives its timeout is recorded as ``timeout`` and abandoned — Python cannot
kill a thread, so the log says the worker was left running rather than pretending it stopped.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (jobs: Sequence[Job], solver: Any = None, on_outcome: Callable[[Outcome], None] | None = None) -> Iterator[Outcome]

classes.name: SlurmBackend
classes.sig: (*, runner: CommandRunner = subprocess_runner, partition: str | None = None, header: Sequence[str] = (), poll_s: float = 5.0, nodes: int = 1, cores_per_run: int = 1)
classes.doc:
SLURM: one ``sbatch`` per job, one ``squeue``/``sacct`` poll for all of them.

The command line of the job is its own ``command`` (or the solver must be a command); the job is expected to
write ``outputs.json`` in its work directory, which is the same contract the local backend uses for command
jobs, so a campaign moves between them without being rewritten. Concurrency, cores per run and the wall-clock
limit come from the same configuration through ``--cpus-per-task`` and ``--time``.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (jobs: Sequence[Job], solver: Any = None, on_outcome: Callable[[Outcome], None] | None = None) -> Iterator[Outcome]

classes.name: CloudBatchBackend
classes.sig: (submit: Callable[[Job], str], poll: Callable[[Sequence[str]], Mapping[str, str]], *, cores_per_run: int = 1, poll_s: float = 10.0)
classes.doc:
One cloud batch service behind the same contract: ``submit`` a job, ``poll`` until it is done.

The service is injected as two callables (``submit(job) -> id`` and ``poll(ids) -> {id: state}``) because the
useful part of this backend is the contract, not the vendor: the campaign passes jobs, gets states and reads the
``outputs.json`` the job wrote to its work directory. :func:`aws_batch_backend` is the adapter for AWS Batch
through the ``aws`` CLI. It was **not** exercised against a real account: the submit/poll calls are tested, the
vendor's answer is not, and a campaign that needs S3 between the job and the work directory must provide it.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (jobs: Sequence[Job], solver: Any = None, on_outcome: Callable[[Outcome], None] | None = None) -> Iterator[Outcome]

classes.name: CampaignReport
classes.doc: What the campaign cost and what it ran on: the accounting the dataset is written with.

classes.name: CampaignResult
classes.doc: The dataset (one row per case) plus the report and the lineage it was produced with.

methods.name: save
methods.doc: Write ``results.json``, ``campaign_report.json`` and ``lineage.json`` next to each other.

classes.name: Campaign
classes.sig: (cases: Sequence[Case], solver: Any, *, name: str = 'campaign', backend: Any = 'local', workers: int = 4, cores_per_run: int = 1, cache_dir: str | Path | None = None, workroot: str | Path | None = None, max_attempts: int = 2, timeout_s: float | None = None, retry_on: Sequence[str] = TRANSIENT_FAILURES, cleanup: bool = True, runner: CommandRunner = subprocess_runner)
classes.doc:
A list of cases and the queue that runs them, once, on the backend it is given.

The order of work is: address every case by its content, answer what the cache proves, run one job per remaining
address with retries, keep every outcome (successful or not) in ``results.json``, and account for the whole
thing. Each finished run is stored as it finishes, so a campaign interrupted at case 900 of 2000 resumes with
the 900 already proven.

methods.name: plan
methods.doc: ``[(case, key, cache record or None)]`` and the keys that are answered by a proven record.

functions.name: case_key
functions.sig: (case: Case, *, solver: str = '', version: str = KEY_VERSION) -> str
functions.doc: The content address of one run: geometry + solver settings + conditions (+ the solver's identity).

functions.name: classify_failure
functions.sig: (log_text: str = '', *, timed_out: bool = False, error: str = '') -> str

functions.name: subprocess_runner
functions.sig: (argv: Sequence[str], *, cwd: str | None = None, timeout: float | None = None) -> CommandResult
functions.doc: The default :class:`CommandRunner`: one local subprocess, its output captured, its timeout enforced.

functions.name: aws_batch_backend
functions.sig: (*, job_queue: str, job_definition: str, runner: CommandRunner = subprocess_runner, region: str | None = None, cores_per_run: int = 1, poll_s: float = 10.0) -> CloudBatchBackend
functions.doc: The AWS Batch adapter: ``aws batch submit-job`` and ``aws batch describe-jobs`` through the CLI.

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (cases: Sequence[Case], solver: Any = None, *, backend: Any = 'local', workers: int = 4, cores_per_run: int = 1, cache_dir: str | Path | None = None, workroot: str | Path | None = None, name: str = 'campaign', max_attempts: int = 2, timeout_s: float | None = None, retry_on: Sequence[str] = TRANSIENT_FAILURES) -> CampaignResult
functions.doc:
Run a campaign: the short form of ``Campaign(...).run()`` (``pp.campaign.run``).

``backend`` is ``"local"``, ``"slurm"``, or a backend instance (``CloudBatchBackend``, ``aws_batch_backend``).
``cache_dir`` turns on content-addressed caching, which is what makes a repeated or resumed campaign cheap.

pinneapple_orchestration.common.provenance
children.doc:
pinneapple_orchestration.common.provenance — ``flow_run_manifest()``: a
context manager every flow in this package wraps its body in, writing
``<manifest_dir>/<flow_name>/<run_id>.json`` on completion (success or
failure): parameters, this repo's own git SHA at run time, a per-task
status log, and any named artifacts — independent of whatever a real
Prefect server's own database retains (and available even when Prefect
isn't installed at all, since ``_prefect_compat`` may be running the flow
as a plain function).

functions.name: flow_run_manifest
functions.sig: (flow_name: str, parameters: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, *, manifest_dir: str = 'data/manifests', repo_dir: Optional[str] = None) -> Iterator[FlowRunManifest]
functions.doc:
Usage::

with flow_run_manifest("flow_02_training", {"component": "PipeVanillaPINN"}) as manifest:
    manifest.log_task("build_component", "ok")
    ...
    manifest.add_artifact("model_version", version)

children.name: pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.data_generation_tasks
children.doc:
pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.data_generation_tasks — the task behind
flow_01_data_generation.

Generic on purpose: solvers registered in ``pinneapple_simulation
.numerical_solvers.SolverRegistry`` take wildly different constructor and
call kwargs (an FDM heat solver's inputs look nothing like an SPH
particle solver's), so this task does not try to auto-configure an
arbitrary registered solver. Instead the caller supplies a zero-argument
``sample_fn() -> (coords, fields)`` thunk — in real use this would close
over a call like ``SolverRegistry.build("fdm", ...)(...)`` — and this
task's job is purely to run it N times and persist each run into a
``DatasetStore``.

functions.sig: (dataset_store: DatasetStore, problem_id: str, sample_fn: SampleFn, n_scenarios: int, *, scenario_prefix: str = 'scenario') -> List[str]
functions.doc:
Runs ``sample_fn()`` ``n_scenarios`` times and saves each result as
a new scenario. Returns the list of saved scenario ids.

children.name: pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.digital_twin_tasks
children.doc:
pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.digital_twin_tasks — the task behind
flow_05_digital_twin_prep.

Gated on stage: by default only a model already promoted to
``"production"`` in the registry (see ``registry_tasks.publish_model_task``)
can be prepped into a live ``DigitalTwin`` — mirroring the same
stage-promotion discipline the registry itself enforces, so a
still-``"development"``/``"staging"`` model can't accidentally end up
driving what looks like a production twin.

functions.name: prepare_digital_twin_task
functions.sig: (registry: ArtifactRegistry, problem_id: str, field_names: list[str], coord_names: list[str] | None = None, *, version: str | None = None, require_stage: str | None = 'production', model_cls: Any | None = None, config: DigitalTwinConfig | None = None, **init_kwargs) -> DigitalTwin

children.name: pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.registry_tasks
children.doc:
pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.registry_tasks — the task behind
flow_04_registry_publish, the terminal "promote to a real stage" step.

Requires an explicit ``confirm=True``, the same human-confirmation gate a
sibling internal project's own library-publishing flow used for its
terminal step — a stage promotion (especially to ``"production"``) is
exactly the kind of action that should never happen as a side effect of
an otherwise-automated pipeline running to completion.

functions.name: publish_model_task
functions.sig: (registry: ArtifactRegistry, problem_id: str, model: Any, *, metadata: dict[str, Any] | None = None, stage: str = 'staging', confirm: bool = False, trust_report: Any | None = None, override_reason: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Saves ``model`` into ``registry.models`` and (only if
``confirm=True``) promotes it to ``stage``. Raises ``PermissionError``
if ``confirm`` is not explicitly ``True`` and ``stage`` is anything
other than ``"development"`` — the default, un-promoted stage a plain
``save()`` already lands on. A REJECT ``trust_report`` blocks the
promotion unless ``override_reason`` is given (decision D2).

children.summary: The task behind flow_04_registry_publish, the terminal "promote to a real stage" step.

children.name: pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.training_tasks
children.doc:
pinneapple_orchestration.tasks.training_tasks — the task behind
flow_02_training. Thin: builds a component via ``ComponentRegistry`` and
delegates to ``ComponentModel.fit()`` (which itself delegates to the
shared ``Trainer``) — no training loop lives here. Also logs the run into
an ``ExperimentStore`` so it's queryable later independent of this flow's
own manifest file.

functions.name: train_component_task
functions.sig: (component_name: str, train_loader: Any, val_loader: Any | None = None, *, experiment_store: ExperimentStore | None = None, epochs: int = 100, lr: float = 0.001, log_dir: str | None = None, **build_kwargs) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Builds ``component_name`` via ``ComponentRegistry``, trains it, and
(if ``experiment_store`` is given) logs the run. Returns a dict with
the trained ``model`` plus ``Trainer.fit()``'s own result dict.

children.summary: The tasks the flows are made of.

doc:
pinneapple_orchestration — an optional Prefect-based pipeline layer
wiring together capabilities that already exist elsewhere in PINNeAPPle:
``pinneapple_registry`` (artifact storage), ``pinneapple_systems
.component_library`` (trainable components), and ``pinneapple_systems
.digital_twin``. No orchestration layer (Prefect, Airflow, or otherwise)
previously existed anywhere in this repo — confirmed via repo-wide grep.

Kept deliberately lean — five flows, not a large numbered pipeline suite,
since this is a generic library, not a single product with a fixed
vertical pipeline:

1. ``flow_data_generation``  — sample scenarios via a caller-supplied
   solver thunk, persist into ``DatasetStore``.
2. ``flow_training``         — build + train a registered component,
   log the run into ``ExperimentStore``.
3. ``flow_benchmark``        — rank every architecture registered for a
   ``component_type``.
4. ``flow_registry_publish`` — the terminal, human-confirmed stage
   promotion (``development`` -> ``staging``/``production``).
5. ``flow_digital_twin_prep``— build a live ``DigitalTwin`` from a
   registry-stored, stage-gated model.

Real Prefect (retries, scheduling, a UI, deployments) is available once
you ``pip install "pinneapple[orchestration]"``; without it, every flow
and task here is still a plain, directly callable Python function (see
``_prefect_compat.py``) — nothing in this package requires Prefect to be
usable or testable.

    from pinneapple_orchestration.flows import flow_training
    from pinneapple_registry import ArtifactRegistry

    registry = ArtifactRegistry("./my_registry")
    result = flow_training("PipeVanillaPINN", train_loader, val_loader,
                            experiment_store=registry.experiments, epochs=50)
summary: An optional Prefect-based pipeline layer wiring together capabilities that already exist elsewhere in PINNeAPPle: pinneapple_registry (artifact storage), pinneapple_systems .component_library ...
